source_text: CAPUT QUINTUM, De satisfactione Christi. Hic de statibus Christi sequitur SATISFACTIO, qua Filius Dei per gratiam miserationis a Patre virtute Spiritus sancti incarnatus nobis in melioris foederis Sponforem concessus, seque in pretium redemtionis pro nobis dependens, perfecta obedientia sui, quae in humiliatione reperitur, inobedientiam humani generis vere ac plene compensavit, adeoque meritus est & effecit, ut salva DEI iustitia, omnes peccatores in ipsum credentes remissionem peccatorum & vitam aeternam actu consequerentur, ceteri vero, si resipiscerent & crederent, certo consequi possent. Sedes huius principii est Rom. 3:24-25; 5:6,9,16-19; 8:1; 1 Cor. 1:30; 15:22; 2 Cor. 5:21; Isa. 53:4; Joh. 1:29; Eph. 1:7; 5:2; Col. 1:14; 1 Thess. 1:10; 1 Tim. 2:6; Heb. 7:22; 9:12; 10:12; 1 Pet. 1:18-19; 2:24; 2 Pet. 2:1; Apoc. 5:9; Matth. 20:28; Marci 10:45.
english: CHAPTER FIVE. On the satisfaction of Christ.

Here, after the states of Christ, follows SATISFACTION, by which the Son of God, incarnate by the grace of mercy from the Father through the power of the Holy Spirit, granted to us as Sponsor of the better covenant, and paying Himself as the price of redemption for us, by His perfect obedience found in humiliation, truly and fully compensated the disobedience of the human race, and so merited and effected that, the justice of GOD being preserved, all sinners who believe in Him actually obtain remission of sins and eternal life, while the rest, if they repent and believe, can certainly obtain it.

The seat of this principle is Romans 3:24-25; 5:6,9,16-19; 8:1; 1 Corinthians 1:30; 15:22; 2 Corinthians 5:21; Isaiah 53:4; John 1:29; Ephesians 1:7; 5:2; Colossians 1:14; 1 Thessalonians 1:10; 1 Timothy 2:6; Hebrews 7:22; 9:12; 10:12; 1 Peter 1:18-19; 2:24; 2 Peter 2:1; Revelation 5:9; Matthew 20:28; Mark 10:45.

source_text: Quam partem doctrinae Christianae omnium vehementissime impugnavit nimis infaustus Faustus Socinus libris suis de mediatore servatore nostro Domino Jesu Christo, cui opponimus eruditissimum scriptum Hugonis Grotii de satisfactione, aliorumque ad hoc scriptum notationes eruditas & orthodoxas, juxta cum iis quae doctissimus D. Constantinus L'Empereur in hoc argumento contra Judaeos disserit ad Esaiam & alibi. Et quod Pontificii hic labefactant, id assertum vide post Lutherum passim et Calv. L. 3 Inst. c. 4.25-26, a nobilissimo Theologo Antonio Sadeele aliisque orthodoxis scriptoribus, bene contra merita & satisfactiones humanas passim & solide scribentibus. Ceterum inter orthodoxos minime controversum esse debet: 1. Non nudum hominem, sed ipsum Dei Filium pro nobis passum & mortuum, non secundum nudam & externam denominationem duntaxat, sed revera & ipso opere. Sicut enim Dei Filius revera nostra causa factus est homo, ita etiam Dei Filius vere ac reipsa pro nobis est mortuus. Ex quo tamen II. minime sequitur, quod etiam Deitas vel Christus secundum Deitatem proprie passus & mortuus sit. Aliud enim est, si quaeras: quis pro nobis passus & mortuus sit? Et aliud: in qua sive secundum quam naturam proprie mortuus sit? Si enim de persona quaeras quae pro nobis passa est, respondeo cum Petro Act. 3:15 eos principem vitae interfecisse; & cum Paulo 1 Cor. 2:8 eos Dominum gloriae crucifixisse; & Act. 20:28 Deum ipsum ecclesiam proprio suo sanguine acquisivisse; & Gal. 2:20 Filius Dei dilexit me, tradidit se pro me. Si vero quaeras de natura in qua vel secundum quam passus est, respondeo cum Petro, occisum esse secundum carnem, 1 Pet. 3:18; passum pro nobis in carne, 1 Pet. 4:1; obtulisse peccata nostra in corpore suo, 1 Pet. 2:24. Deitas enim est & manet per se immortalis nullique passioni obnoxia: & nihilominus tamen est ac dicitur Filii Dei propria passio, quia in proprio corpore suo passus est, propriumque sanguinem suum effudit.
english: This part of Christian doctrine Faustus Socinus, most unhappy of men, attacked most vehemently of all in his books on our mediator and Savior the Lord Jesus Christ. Against him we set Hugo Grotius's most learned writing On Satisfaction, and the learned and orthodox notes of others on that writing, together with what the most learned Constantijn L'Empereur discusses on this argument against the Jews on Isaiah and elsewhere. And what the papal writers undermine here, see asserted after Luther everywhere and Calvin, Institutes 3.4.25-26, by the most noble theologian Antoine de Chandieu (Sadeel) and other orthodox writers who write well and solidly against human merits and satisfactions.

Moreover among the orthodox it ought least of all to be controversial: 1. Not a bare man, but the Son of God Himself suffered and died for us, not according to a bare and external denomination only, but in very deed and in the work itself. For just as the Son of God truly became man for our sake, so also the Son of God truly and in reality died for us.

II. From this it by no means follows that the Deity, or Christ according to the Deity, properly suffered and died. For it is one thing to ask who suffered and died for us, and another in which nature, or according to which nature, He properly died. If you ask about the person who suffered for us, I answer with Peter (Acts 3:15) that they killed the Author of life; and with Paul (1 Cor. 2:8) that they crucified the Lord of glory; and Acts 20:28 that God Himself acquired the church with His own blood; and Galatians 2:20: the Son of God loved me and gave Himself for me. But if you ask about the nature in which or according to which He suffered, I answer with Peter that He was killed according to the flesh (1 Pet. 3:18), suffered for us in the flesh (1 Pet. 4:1), and bore our sins in His body (1 Pet. 2:24). For the Deity is and remains of itself immortal and subject to no passion; and yet the passion is and is called the Son of God's own, because He suffered in His own body and poured out His own blood.

source_text: Et III. minime vocandum est in dubium, quod Christus secundum aeternum Dei consilium in hunc finem proprie mortuus sit, & quod plenissimo sacrificio propitiatorio & satisfactione passionis & mortis suae hoc proprie meruerit & impetraverit, quod omnes ac singuli homines, qui in ipsum credunt, propter ipsum remissionem peccatorum & vitam aeternam actu consequantur, ceteri vero omnes ac singuli, si modo resipiscant & credant, certo consequi queant, ut olim respondi ad articulum secundum sive secundum doctrinae caput de morte Christi in synodo Dordracena. Vide judicia Theol. exterorum pag. 127 Dordrechti edita. Quod hic igitur quaeratur, utrum Christus pro omnibus hominibus, an vero non pro omnibus mortuus sit? Utrumque sano & distincto intellectu citra contradictionem dici potest. Nam mortuus est pro omnibus, phrasi scripturae, quantum ad perfectionem & sufficientiam meriti sui & satisfactionis, quia hanc gratiam, quae in Euangelio annunciatur, quod nempe per fidem remissionem peccatorum consequi debeant, pro omnibus hominibus in hoc mundo, imo si eorum & alter mundus esset, plenissime sufficientissime & efficacissime per mortem suam impetravit, ita ut 1. omnibus communiter serio ac bona fide offeratur; 2. ab omnibus vera paenitentia ac fides haud simulate exigatur; & 3. omnibus simul serio propter Christum remissio peccatorum & vita aeterna sub conditione fidei promittatur. Unde & 4. omnes obligati sunt ac tenentur resipiscere ac credere in Christum tanquam Messiam suum & Salvatorem, ut promissionem consequantur.
english: III. Least of all may it be called into doubt that Christ, according to the eternal counsel of God, properly died for this end, and that by the fullest propitiatory sacrifice and the satisfaction of His passion and death He properly merited and obtained this: that each and every human who believes in Him actually obtains, because of Him, remission of sins and eternal life, while each and every other person, if only they repent and believe, can certainly obtain it — as I once answered to the second article, or second chapter of doctrine on the death of Christ, in the Synod of Dort. See the Judgments of the Foreign Theologians, p. 127, published at Dordrecht.

When it is asked whether Christ died for all humans or not for all, both can be said with a sound and distinct sense without contradiction. For He died for all, in the phrasing of Scripture, as to the perfection and sufficiency of His merit and satisfaction, because by His death He most fully, sufficiently, and efficaciously obtained this grace announced in the Gospel — that they ought to obtain remission of sins through faith — for all humans in this world, indeed even if there were another world of them, so that: 1. it is offered in common to all seriously and in good faith; 2. true repentance and unfeigned faith are demanded of all; and 3. remission of sins and eternal life are seriously promised to all together for Christ's sake under the condition of faith. Hence also 4. all are obligated and bound to repent and believe in Christ as their Messiah and Savior, that they may obtain the promise.

source_text: Atque hunc in modum non male asseritur, Deum per mortem Christi toti humano generi eatenus reconciliatum esse, ut omnibus communiter, quamvis natura sint filii irae, nihilominus gratiam suam & reconciliationem in Christo fideliter ac serio offerri velit, 2 Cor. 5:20. Atque ita nullus omnino est ex omnibus hominibus, pro quo Christus non satisfecerit, sicut vere respondit Prosper Pelagianis ad articulos Augustino falso impositos. Quare mors Christi in se, sine fidei consideratione, ad omnes omnino homines, etiam peccatores, inimicos Christi & impios pertinet: fructus vero illius salutaris applicatio nulli nisi fideli tribui potest, quippe cuius instrumentalis causa fides est. Non pro omnibus, sed pro solis credentibus mortuus sit, quantum ad actualem communicationem & applicationem meriti mortis ipsius, quia non omnibus actu pleno prodest, neque eius omnes homines sic reipsa participes fiunt, sed soli illi qui vera fide amplectuntur. Hujus assertionis fundamenta sunt potissima, quod Christus vitam suam posuerit pro ovibus suis, Joh. 10:15; pro amicis, Joh. 15:13; ut filios Dei dispersos colligeret, Joh. 11:52; ut purificaret sibi populum in peculium, Tit. 2:14; ecclesiam sanguine suo redemit, Act. 20:28; pro ecclesia se tradidit, Eph. 5:25. Hoc duntaxat asserunt, Christum non esse mortuum neque ullam reconciliationem impetravisse ac promeruisse infidelibus, quatenus in infidelitate & impenitentia sua obfirmant & in finem perseverant. Qui igitur non credunt, ii, non quidem ob defectum novae gratiae paternae miserationis aut satisfactionis & meriti Christi, sed ob incredulitatem propriam, ab ea excluduntur.
english: And in this way it is not badly asserted that God through the death of Christ has been so far reconciled to the whole human race that He wills His grace and reconciliation in Christ to be offered faithfully and seriously in common to all, even though by nature they are children of wrath (2 Cor. 5:20). And so there is absolutely no one among all humans for whom Christ did not make satisfaction, as Prosper truly answered the Pelagians on the articles falsely imposed on Augustine. Therefore the death of Christ in itself, without consideration of faith, pertains to all humans whatsoever, even sinners, enemies of Christ, and the ungodly; but the saving application of its fruit can be attributed to none except the believer, since faith is its instrumental cause.

He died not for all, but for believers alone, as to the actual communication and application of the merit of His death, because it does not benefit all with full act, nor do all humans thus become real partakers of it, but only those who embrace it with true faith. The chief foundations of this assertion are that Christ laid down His life for His sheep (John 10:15), for friends (John 15:13), that He might gather the scattered children of God (John 11:52), purify for Himself a people as His possession (Titus 2:14), redeemed the church with His blood (Acts 20:28), and gave Himself for the church (Eph. 5:25).

They assert only this: that Christ did not die, nor obtain and merit any reconciliation, for unbelievers insofar as they harden themselves in their unbelief and impenitence and persevere to the end. Those who do not believe, therefore, are excluded from it not because of any defect of the new grace of paternal mercy or of Christ's satisfaction and merit, but because of their own unbelief.

source_text: II. Sunt autem hic quaedam NOTABILIA. 1. Satisfactio & meritum Christi non differunt reipsa ita ut in diversis operationibus debeant quaeri: sed varia ratione, in una eademque obedientia & humiliatione ipsius debent agnosci. Haec enim fuit etiam meritum, qua ordinatur ad commodum nostrum vel ad aliquid boni, sub ratione mercedis, nobis acquirendum, argumento Rom. 5:10,19; 3:25. 2. Satisfactio haec, quantum ad substantiam rei, fuit perfecta ex rigore iustitiae: gratiam tamen supponit, qua vocatus fuit Christus ad opus hoc praestandum, & qua praestitum acceptatum fuit nostro nomine et in bonum nostrum: qua denique ex pacto remunerante perficitur illud, quod in ista satisfactione quaerebatur, Joh. 3:16; Rom. 3:24; 5:15. Atque ita in redemtione humani generis simul lucet summa Dei iustitia & summa gratia, Rom. 5:17, ut satisfactionis huius fructus & effectus omnes simul gratiae & misericordiae Dei recte tribuantur. Vide Joh. Calv.
english: II. Here there are certain NOTABLE points.

1. The satisfaction and merit of Christ do not differ in the thing itself so that they must be sought in diverse operations; but they must be recognized under a varied ratio in one and the same obedience and humiliation of His. For this was also merit, insofar as it is ordered to our benefit or to acquiring something good for us under the ratio of a wage (Rom. 5:10,19; 3:25).

2. This satisfaction, as to the substance of the thing, was perfect from the rigor of justice; yet it presupposes grace, by which Christ was called to perform this work, and by which what was performed was accepted in our name and for our good; and finally by which, from the remunerating covenant, that which was sought in this satisfaction is perfected (John 3:16; Rom. 3:24; 5:15). And so in the redemption of the human race the highest justice of God and the highest grace shine together (Rom. 5:17), so that all the fruits and effects of this satisfaction are rightly attributed at once to the grace and mercy of God. See John Calvin.

source_text: 3. Satisfactionis huius valor est sufficiens & aliqua ratione infinitus. Id probatur 1. a persona offerentis, qui fuit Deus; 2. a dignitate & praestantia rei oblatae. Obtulit enim semetipsum Deum & hominem; 3. a modo offerendi, cui divina quaedam perfectio inest ex hypostatica unione. Quemadmodum enim gravitatem iniuriae auget dignitas personae offensae: ita valor satisfactionis intenditur a dignitate satisfacientis, quia hic cernitur exhibitio honoris, qui pendet e dignitate personae exhibentis. 4. Substantialis dignitas, quae in Christo fuit, magis proprie confert ad dignitatem operis, quam accidentalis, qualis est in hominibus quibusdam prae aliis, principibus nimirum, sapientibus, parentibus. Ad extremum, qui descriptionem satisfactionis plenius explicatam desiderat, is videat synopsin purioris Theologiae Theol. Leidensium disp. 29, Locos communes Wolfg. Musculi & quae pro Augustana confessione ad D. Mentzerum de hoc argumento disseruimus. Dissentiunt hodie cumprimis Photiniani & Socinus de Christo servatore, Smalcius, Georgius Enjedinus, Sommerus, Ostovod, secuti Petrum Abaelardum, qui circa ann. 1140 a nato Christo satisfactionem oppugnavit, cui suffragati sunt Arnoldus de Brixia & Albertus Pictaviensium episcopus atque Servetus Hispanus in hoc Judaizantes. CAPUT SEXTUM sequitur, De gratia supernae & sanctae vocationis.
english: 3. The value of this satisfaction is sufficient and in some respect infinite. That is proved: 1. from the person of the offerer, who was God; 2. from the dignity and excellence of the thing offered — for He offered Himself, God and man; 3. from the mode of offering, to which a certain divine perfection belongs from the hypostatic union. For just as the dignity of the offended person increases the gravity of the injury, so the value of satisfaction is intensified by the dignity of the one who satisfies, because here is seen the exhibition of honor that depends on the dignity of the exhibiting person.

4. The substantial dignity that was in Christ contributes more properly to the dignity of the work than accidental dignity, such as is in certain humans above others — namely princes, the wise, parents. Finally, whoever desires a fuller explanation of the description of satisfaction should see the Synopsis of Purer Theology of the Leiden theologians, disputation 29; Wolfgang Musculus's Common Places; and what we discussed for the Augsburg Confession to D. Mentzer on this argument.

Today especially the Photinians and Socinus On Christ the Savior dissent, with Smalcius, György Enyedi, Sommer, and Ostovod, following Peter Abelard, who around A.D. 1140 attacked satisfaction — to whom Arnold of Brescia and Albert bishop of the Poitevins and the Spaniard Servetus agreed, Judaizing in this.
CHAPTER SIX follows, On the grace of heavenly and holy calling.
